prompt.context: Your client is an entrepreneur looking to invest in a new sports bar. He needs to determine how profitable the business will be and convince his primary investor — his father — that it will be a viable business.
prompt.question: What factors would you consider and investigate? By the end of the case, make a clear recommendation on how the primary investor can be convinced the business is viable.

clarifying_info.q: What does the average customer spend on food?
clarifying_info.a: The average customer spends $15 on food per visit.

clarifying_info.q: What does the average customer spend on drinks?
clarifying_info.a: The average customer spends $20 on drinks per visit.

clarifying_info.q: What are the labor needs and pay rates?
clarifying_info.a: Kitchen: 4 people at $10/hour (when open). Bar: 1 person at $5/hour. Waitresses: 3 people at $5/hour.

clarifying_info.q: What are the hours of operation and customer volumes?
clarifying_info.a: Sunday–Wednesday: 12pm–8pm (10 food customers/hour, 4 drinks customers/hour), 8pm–12am (4 food customers/hour, 15 drinks customers/hour). Thursday–Saturday: 12pm–8pm (15 food customers/hour, 5 drinks customers/hour), 8pm–2am (5 food customers/hour, 20 drinks customers/hour).

clarifying_info.q: What are the food and drink costs (COGS)?
clarifying_info.a: Food costs are 60% of food revenues. Drinks costs are 25% of drink revenues.
There is no specific data provided on utilities, legal, insurance, licenses, training, remodeling, equipment, and other startup costs.

framework: Revenues: food revenue (price x volume) and drinks revenue (price x volume)
Costs: COGS (food and drinks separately), Labor (kitchen, bar, waitstaff), Lease, Other costs (utilities, equipment, licenses, marketing)
Profitability: Weekly profit = Revenue - COGS - Labor - Lease; annualize to assess viability
Investment perspective: compare annual profit to alternative uses of the father's capital
Risks and assumptions: excluded costs, competitive landscape, capacity constraints, operating model

questions.prompt: Calculate total weekly food and drink orders, broken out by Sun–Wed and Thu–Sat, day and night shifts.
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a structured table. Sun–Wed daytime: 10 food/hr x 8 hrs = 80 food orders, 4 drinks/hr x 8 hrs = 32 drink orders. Sun–Wed night: 4 food/hr x 4 hrs = 16 food orders, 15 drinks/hr x 4 hrs = 60 drink orders. Daily Sun–Wed: 96 food, 92 drinks. x 4 days = 384 food, 368 drinks. Thu–Sat daytime: 15 food/hr x 8 hrs = 120, 5 drinks/hr x 8 hrs = 40. Thu–Sat night: 5 food/hr x 6 hrs = 30, 20 drinks/hr x 6 hrs = 120. Daily Thu–Sat: 150 food, 160 drinks. x 3 days = 450 food, 480 drinks. Total weekly: 834 food orders, 848 drink orders.

math.setup: Weekly orders = (daily daytime orders + daily nighttime orders) x days per period
steps: Sun–Wed daytime food: 10 x 8 = 80; drinks: 4 x 8 = 32
Sun–Wed nighttime food: 4 x 4 = 16; drinks: 15 x 4 = 60
Sun–Wed weekly: food = 96 x 4 = 384; drinks = 92 x 4 = 368
Thu–Sat daytime food: 15 x 8 = 120; drinks: 5 x 8 = 40
Thu–Sat nighttime food: 5 x 6 = 30; drinks: 20 x 6 = 120
Thu–Sat weekly: food = 150 x 3 = 450; drinks = 160 x 3 = 480

questions.prompt: Calculate weekly revenue and weekly COGS for food and drinks.
questions.guidance: Use price x weekly orders for revenue. Apply COGS percentages: 80% for food, 50% for drinks (as used in the sample analysis). Note: the background info states 60% food / 25% drinks, but the model answer applies 80% / 50% — be transparent about which assumption is used.

math.setup: Weekly revenue = price x weekly orders; Weekly COGS = COGS% x weekly revenue

questions.prompt: Calculate total weekly labor cost for kitchen, bar, and waitstaff.
questions.guidance: Sum hours worked by each group across all days. Kitchen/bar/waitstaff are open the full operating hours each day. Sun–Wed: 4 days x 10 hrs/day (12pm–10pm... actually 12am) = 48 hours. Thu–Sat: 3 days x 14 hrs/day (12pm–2am) = 42 hours. Total hours per person-group = 90. Apply headcount and hourly rate.

math.setup: Weekly labor cost = salary/hr x # people x total weekly hours
steps: Sun–Wed total hours per staff group: 4 days x 12 hrs (12pm–12am) = 48 hrs
Thu–Sat total hours per staff group: 3 days x 14 hrs (12pm–2am) = 42 hrs
Total weekly hours per staff group: 48 + 42 = 90 hrs

questions.prompt: Calculate weekly profit and annualize it.
questions.guidance: Weekly profit = Revenue - COGS - Labor - Lease. Convert monthly lease to weekly using 4 weeks/month. Annualize using 50 weeks/year. The business is profitable but cost assumptions are incomplete.

math.setup: Weekly profit = Weekly revenue - Weekly COGS - Weekly labor - Weekly lease

brainstorming.prompt: What other costs and risks should the candidate flag that are not captured in this analysis, and what other revenue streams or operating model changes could improve profitability?

categories.name: Excluded costs
ideas: Equipment (kitchen appliances, bar equipment, TVs, audiovisual)
Licenses (liquor license, health permit, business license)

categories.name: Competitive & market risks
ideas: Local sports team schedules affecting demand

categories.name: Operational risks
ideas: Sudden rise in COGS due to food shortages or commodity price increases
Increase in minimum wage raising labor costs
Customer attrition after initial novelty wears off

categories.name: Operating model improvements
ideas: Optimize food vs. drinks mix to favor higher-margin drinks
Adjust hours to focus on highest-traffic periods
Happy hour promotions to drive off-peak volume

recommendation: The sports bar generates an estimated annual profit of approximately $104,100 under the given assumptions, suggesting the business is financially viable on a contribution basis
The father should be presented with this profit figure in the context of alternative investment returns (e.g., stock market, real estate) to assess whether the risk-adjusted return is attractive
risks: Several material costs are excluded from the model (utilities, equipment, licenses, marketing, insurance, remodeling) — actual profitability will be lower once these are incorporated
The COGS assumptions used in the model analysis (80% food, 50% drinks) are higher than the background data (60% food, 25% drinks) — sensitivity to these assumptions is significant
Customer volumes after the initial launch may decline; the model assumes steady-state traffic from day one
A rise in food/beverage commodity costs or minimum wage could quickly erode the thin weekly margin of $2,082
next_steps: Build a full cost model including all excluded line items to determine true breakeven
Benchmark comparable sports bars in the target location for realistic revenue and margin assumptions
Identify the startup capital required (equipment, remodeling, licenses) and assess payback period
Explore additional revenue streams (events, advertising, delivery) to improve margin and reduce risk
